```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r load_packages}
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, janitor, nnet,caret,MASS,pROC, rsample)
```

```{r read_data, warning=FALSE}
fraud_data <- read_csv("Digital_Payment_Fraud_Detection_Dataset.csv")
fraud_data <- clean_names(fraud_data)

fraud_data <- fraud_data |>
  mutate(
    fraud_label = as.factor(fraud_label),
    transaction_type = as.factor(transaction_type),
    payment_mode = as.factor(payment_mode),
    device_type = as.factor(device_type),
    is_international = as.factor(is_international),
    device_location = as.factor(device_location)    
  )|>
  dplyr::select(-c(transaction_id,user_id))

levels(fraud_data$fraud_label) <- make.names(levels(fraud_data$fraud_label))

glimpse(fraud_data)
```


```{r split_data}
set.seed(2026)
d1 <- fraud_data|>
  group_by(fraud_label)|>
  sample_frac(0.8)

test <- anti_join(fraud_data,d1)
train <- d1|>
  group_by(fraud_label)|>
  sample_frac(0.8)
validation <- anti_join(d1,train)
```

## Logistic Regression

Since the decision threshold of 0.5 is no good in this dataset, I need to find an optimal threshold value. I will use ROC curves to determine this.

SOURCE: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/deciding-threshold-for-glm-logistic-regression-model-in-r/

### Second Logistic Model

This time we will add weights to each class, since data is so unbalanced

```{r logistic_model2}
logistic2 <- glm(fraud_label ~ transaction_amount+device_location+account_age_days+is_international+ip_risk_score+login_attempts_last_24h, data=train, family = "binomial", weights = ifelse(train$fraud_label == "X1", 5, 1))


Lprobs2 <- predict(logistic2,validation,type="response")

Pred2 <- ifelse(Lprobs2 >= 0.2481125, "X1", "X0") # use ROC to determine optimal threshold

Pred2 <- factor(Pred2, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

Actual2 <- factor(validation$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

confusionMatrix(Pred2, Actual2, positive = "X1")
```

### Third Logistic Model

Using linear transformations and find interaction between variables to create best logistic model possible, 
https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/splines/versions/3.6.2/topics/ns

```{r logistic_model3}
library(splines)

logistic3 <- glm(fraud_label ~ 
                   ns(ip_risk_score, 3) +
                   ns(account_age_days, 3) +
                   previous_failed_attempts,
                 data = train,
                 family = "binomial",
                 weights = ifelse(train$fraud_label == "X1", 5, 1))

Lprobs3 <- predict(logistic3,validation,type="response")

# find optimal threshold

# roc_obj <- roc(validation$fraud_label, Lprobs3)
# plot(roc_obj)
# 
# coords(roc_obj, "best", ret = "threshold")

Pred3 <- ifelse(Lprobs3 >= 0.2623522, "X1", "X0") 

Pred3 <- factor(Pred3, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

Actual3 <- factor(validation$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

confusionMatrix(Pred3, Actual3, positive = "X1")

```

### Test Best Logistic Model

I would say that the third logistic model is the best one, it has the highest balanced accuracy. I believe that logistic model is not good at this type of classification problem since none of the 3 models performed very well.

```{r best_logistic}
LprobsB <- predict(logistic3,test,type="response")

# find optimal threshold

# roc_obj <- roc(test$fraud_label, LprobsB)
# plot(roc_obj)
# 
# coords(roc_obj, "best", ret = "threshold")

PredB <- ifelse(LprobsB >= 0.2280686, "X1", "X0") 

PredB <- factor(PredB, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

ActualB <- factor(test$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

cm_log <- confusionMatrix(PredB, ActualB, positive = "X1")

```

## KNN

### First KNN Model

I do not need to scale the data since the preProcess command and predict command already do that. I will also use ROC to find the optimal threshold for the same reasons as the logistic model

```{r knn}
library(caret)

set.seed(2026)

# make sure response levels are correct
train$fraud_label <- factor(train$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))
validation$fraud_label <- factor(validation$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

# 10-fold cross validation
ctrl_kfold <- caret::trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 10,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = caret::twoClassSummary
)

# values of k to try
knn_grid <- expand.grid(k = 1:20)

# fit baseline KNN
knn_model1 <- caret::train(
  fraud_label ~ .,
  data = train,
  method = "knn",
  tuneGrid = knn_grid,
  trControl = ctrl_kfold,
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
  metric = "ROC"
)

# look at results
print(knn_model1)
plot(knn_model1)
knn_model1$bestTune

# default class predictions on validation set
final_pred <- predict(knn_model1, newdata = validation)

# confusion matrix
caret::confusionMatrix(final_pred, validation$fraud_label, positive = "X1")
```

### Second KNN Model

Goal of this mode is to improve detection of fraud (class X1). For my Knn models I noticed that using the ROC curve just brings about a lot of errors, so instead I am using a for loop to check a bunch of possible thresholds and then picking the best. In this model i am using down sampling, i tested up sampling and it did not work well

```{r knn2}
library(caret)

set.seed(2026)

actual <- factor(validation$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

ctrl_kfold2 <- caret::trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 10,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = caret::twoClassSummary,
  sampling = "down"
)

kknn_grid <- expand.grid(
  kmax = seq(3, 25, by = 2),
  distance = c(1, 2),
  kernel = c("rectangular", "triangular", "optimal")
)

knn_model2 <- caret::train(
  fraud_label ~ ip_risk_score + previous_failed_attempts + account_age_days,
  data = train,
  method = "kknn",
  tuneGrid = kknn_grid,
  trControl = ctrl_kfold2,
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
  metric = "ROC"
)

print(knn_model2)
knn_model2$bestTune

knn_probs2 <- predict(knn_model2, newdata = validation, type = "prob")[, "X1"]

results <- data.frame()

for (t in seq(0.05, 0.30, by = 0.01)) {
  pred <- factor(ifelse(knn_probs2 >= t, "X1", "X0"),
                 levels = c("X0", "X1"))

  cm <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred, actual, positive = "X1")

  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    threshold = t,
    sensitivity = cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
    specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    precision = cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
    F1 = cm$byClass["F1"]
  ))
}

results[order(-results$F1), ]

# apply threshold = 0.19
final_pred2 <- ifelse(knn_probs2 >= 0.19, "X1", "X0")
final_pred2 <- factor(final_pred2, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

# confusion matrix
caret::confusionMatrix(final_pred2, actual, positive = "X1")

```

### Third KNN Model

In my second model the sensitivity is good but it is predicting too many as fraudulent, giving it a very poor accuracy and F1

```{r knn3}

# cross-validation setup
ctrl_kfold3 <- caret::trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 10,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = caret::twoClassSummary,
  sampling = "down"
)

# tuning grid
kknn_grid <- expand.grid(
  kmax = seq(5, 25, by = 2),
  distance = c(1, 2),
  kernel = c("rectangular", "triangular", "optimal")
)

# final KNN model
knn_model3 <- caret::train(
  fraud_label ~ ip_risk_score + previous_failed_attempts + account_age_days,
  data = train,
  method = "kknn",
  tuneGrid = kknn_grid,
  trControl = ctrl_kfold3,
  preProcess = c("center", "scale"),
  metric = "ROC"
)

print(knn_model3)
plot(knn_model3)
knn_model3$bestTune

# predicted probabilities for fraud
knn_probs3 <- predict(knn_model3, newdata = validation, type = "prob")[, "X1"]

# threshold search
results <- data.frame()

for (t in seq(0.05, 0.40, by = 0.01)) {
  
  pred <- factor(ifelse(knn_probs3 >= t, "X1", "X0"),
                 levels = c("X0", "X1"))
  
  cm <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred, actual, positive = "X1")
  
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    threshold = t,
    sensitivity = cm$byClass["Sensitivity"],
    specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    precision = cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
    F1 = cm$byClass["F1"],
    accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"]
  ))
}

results_filtered <- results[results$precision >= 0.10, ]

if (nrow(results_filtered) == 0) {
  best_row <- results[which.max(results$F1), ]
} else {
  best_row <- results_filtered[which.max(results_filtered$F1), ]
}

best_t <- best_row$threshold
best_t

final_pred3 <- factor(ifelse(knn_probs3 >= best_t, "X1", "X0"),
                      levels = c("X0", "X1"))

caret::confusionMatrix(final_pred3, actual, positive = "X1")
```

### Test Best KNN

The third KNN model does perform the best however does not perform well. This has led me to concluding that KNN is not a very good model choice for this type of problem.

```{r knn_test}


# get predicted probabilities for fraud (X1)
knn_probs_test <- predict(knn_model3, newdata = test, type = "prob")[, "X1"]

# actual values
actual_test <- factor(test$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

# apply chosen threshold (replace best_t if needed)
best_t <- best_t  # or manually: best_t <- 0.30 (example)

# predicted classes
knn_pred_test <- ifelse(knn_probs_test >= best_t, "X1", "X0")
knn_pred_test <- factor(knn_pred_test, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

# confusion matrix
cm_knn <- caret::confusionMatrix(knn_pred_test, actual_test, positive = "X1")

cm_knn
```



## Decision Trees

For decision trees, I need to redo my data, use initial_split command instead of group_by for stratification (rsample)

Both boostin, bart required numeric values 0-no , 1-yes, for y variable
randomForest keep factor

need to find class using probability value obtained from prediction

```{r data_for_trees}
set.seed(20)

split_data <- initial_split(fraud_data, prop = 0.8, strata = fraud_label)

train_tree_no_cv <- training(split_data)
test_tree <- testing(split_data)

split2 <- initial_split(train_tree_no_cv, prop = 0.8, strata = fraud_label)
train_tree <- training(split2)
validation_tree <- testing(split2)

```

```{r basic_tree, warning = FALSE}
library(tree)

tree_model <- tree(fraud_label ~ ., data = train_tree)

tree_predictions <- predict(tree_model, newdata = validation_tree, type = "class")
tree_predictions <- factor(tree_predictions, levels = levels(validation_tree$fraud_label))

confusionMatrix(tree_predictions, validation_tree$fraud_label)
```

### Random Forest

mtry = sqrt(p), sqrt(12) = approx 3

oob code : https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/r-machine-learning/how-to-calculate-the-oob-of-random-forest-in-r/

```{r random_forest, warning=FALSE}
library(randomForest)

rf_model <- randomForest(fraud_label ~ ., data=train_tree_no_cv, mtry=3, importance=TRUE)

# OOB error rate
oob_error_rate <- rf_model$err.rate[nrow(rf_model$err.rate), "OOB"]
print(paste("OOB Error Rate:", round(oob_error_rate * 100, 2), "%"))

# Confusion matrix
confusion_matrix <- rf_model$confusion
print(confusion_matrix)

varImpPlot(rf_model)
head(importance(rf_model),5)
```

### Second Random Forest Model 

Built using the 5 most "important" variables from previous model

```{r random_forest2}
library(randomForest)

set.seed(2026)

# make sure response is a factor with correct order
train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label <- factor(train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label,
                                       levels = c("X0", "X1"))

rf_model2 <- randomForest(
  fraud_label ~ transaction_amount + transaction_type + payment_mode + 
    device_type + device_location,
  data = train_tree_no_cv,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = 2,
  importance = TRUE,
  proximity = FALSE
)

# final OOB error rate
oob_error_rate <- rf_model2$err.rate[nrow(rf_model2$err.rate), "OOB"]
cat("OOB Error Rate:", round(oob_error_rate * 100, 2), "%\n")

# OOB confusion matrix stored in the model
confusion_matrix <- rf_model2$confusion
print(confusion_matrix)

# variable importance
var_importance <- importance(rf_model2)
print(var_importance)

# optional importance plot
varImpPlot(rf_model2)

# optional OOB error plot
plot(rf_model2)
```

### Random Forest Model 3

The second model only learned to predict X0. For this model I want to balance classes so that each tree learns on fraud cases.

```{r randomForest3}

set.seed(2026)

# make sure response is a factor
train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label <- factor(train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label,
                                       levels = c("X0", "X1"))

# class counts
class_counts <- table(train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label)
minority_n <- min(class_counts)

rf_model3 <- randomForest(
  fraud_label ~ transaction_amount + transaction_type + payment_mode + 
    device_type + device_location,
  data = train_tree_no_cv,
  ntree = 1000,
  mtry = 2,
  importance = TRUE,
  strata = train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label,
  sampsize = c(minority_n, minority_n),
  nodesize = 1
)

# final OOB error rate
oob_error_rate3 <- rf_model3$err.rate[nrow(rf_model3$err.rate), "OOB"]
cat("OOB Error Rate:", round(oob_error_rate3 * 100, 2), "%\n")

# OOB confusion matrix
confusion_matrix3 <- rf_model3$confusion
print(confusion_matrix3)

# variable importance
var_importance3 <- importance(rf_model3)
print(var_importance3)

# optional plots
varImpPlot(rf_model3)
plot(rf_model3)
```
### RandomForest Model 4

Change some parameters, use different mtry and play around with threshold values. This model performs very well 

```{r randomForest4}
library(randomForest)
library(caret)

set.seed(2026)


# class counts
class_counts <- table(train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label)
minority_n <- min(class_counts)

# less aggressive balanced sampling than model 3
rf_model4 <- randomForest(
  fraud_label ~ transaction_amount + transaction_type + payment_mode +
    device_type + device_location,
  data = train_tree_no_cv,
  ntree = 1000,
  mtry = 3,
  importance = TRUE,
  strata = train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label,
  sampsize = c(minority_n * 2, minority_n),
  nodesize = 1
)

# OOB error rate
oob_error_rate4 <- rf_model4$err.rate[nrow(rf_model4$err.rate), "OOB"]
cat("OOB Error Rate:", round(oob_error_rate4 * 100, 2), "%\n")

# OOB confusion matrix from model
confusion_matrix4 <- rf_model4$confusion
print(confusion_matrix4)

# variable importance
print(importance(rf_model4))
varImpPlot(rf_model4)

# OOB error plot
plot(rf_model4)



rf_probs4 <- predict(rf_model4, newdata = train_tree_no_cv, type = "prob")[, "X1"]

actual4 <- factor(train_tree_no_cv$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

threshold_results4 <- data.frame()

for (t in seq(0.10, 0.50, by = 0.05)) {
  
  pred_t <- factor(ifelse(rf_probs4 >= t, "X1", "X0"),
                   levels = c("X0", "X1"))
  
  cm_t <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred_t, actual4, positive = "X1")
  
  threshold_results4 <- rbind(
    threshold_results4,
    data.frame(
      threshold = t,
      sensitivity = cm_t$byClass["Sensitivity"],
      specificity = cm_t$byClass["Specificity"],
      precision   = cm_t$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
      F1          = cm_t$byClass["F1"],
      accuracy    = cm_t$overall["Accuracy"]
    )
  )
}

threshold_results4
threshold_results4[order(-threshold_results4$F1), ]


threshold_results4_fine <- data.frame()

for (t in seq(0.05, 0.90, by = 0.01)) {
  
  pred_t <- factor(ifelse(rf_probs4 >= t, "X1", "X0"),
                   levels = c("X0", "X1"))
  
  cm_t <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred_t, actual4, positive = "X1")
  
  threshold_results4_fine <- rbind(
    threshold_results4_fine,
    data.frame(
      threshold = t,
      sensitivity = cm_t$byClass["Sensitivity"],
      specificity = cm_t$byClass["Specificity"],
      precision   = cm_t$byClass["Pos Pred Value"],
      F1          = cm_t$byClass["F1"],
      accuracy    = cm_t$overall["Accuracy"]
    )
  )
}

threshold_results4_fine[order(-threshold_results4_fine$F1), ]


best_t4 <- threshold_results4_fine$threshold[which.max(threshold_results4_fine$F1)]
best_t4

final_pred4 <- factor(ifelse(rf_probs4 >= best_t4, "X1", "X0"),
                      levels = c("X0", "X1"))

cm_rf4 <- caret::confusionMatrix(final_pred4, actual4, positive = "X1")
cm_rf4

```

### Test Best Tree Model

RF model 4 was the best by far, however it overfitted on this data

```{r testRandomForest}
rf_probs_test <- predict(rf_model4, newdata = test_tree, type = "prob")[, "X1"]

actual_test <- factor(test_tree$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

final_pred_test <- factor(ifelse(rf_probs_test >= 0.59, "X1", "X0"),
                          levels = c("X0", "X1"))

cm_rf <- caret::confusionMatrix(final_pred_test, actual_test, positive = "X1")
```


## Boosting/BART

### Boosting

```{r boosting, warning=FALSE}
library(gbm)

# change y var to make numeric
boost_train <- d1|>
  mutate(fraud_label = ifelse(fraud_label == "X0", 0,1))
boost_test <- test|>
  mutate(fraud_label = ifelse(fraud_label == "X0", 0,1))

boost_model <- gbm(fraud_label ~ ., data = boost_train, distribution = "bernoulli", n.trees = 5000, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage= 0.001)

yhat_boost <- predict(boost_model, newdata = boost_test, n.trees = 5000, type = "response")

actual <- factor(boost_test$fraud_label)

roc_obj <- roc(actual, yhat_boost, levels = c(0, 1))

best_thresh <- as.numeric(coords(roc_obj, "best", ret = "threshold"))
best_thresh

yhat_class <- ifelse(yhat_boost > best_thresh, 1, 0) 

confusionMatrix(as.factor(yhat_class),as.factor(boost_test$fraud_label))



```

### BART



```{r bart}
library(BART)
library(caret)
library(pROC)

boost_train <- d1 |>
  mutate(fraud_label = ifelse(fraud_label == "X0", 0, 1))

boost_test <- test |>
  mutate(fraud_label = ifelse(fraud_label == "X0", 0, 1))

# Create numeric design matrices
xtrain <- model.matrix(fraud_label ~ . - 1, data = boost_train)
xtest  <- model.matrix(fraud_label ~ . - 1, data = boost_test)

# Response as numeric vector
ytrain <- boost_train$fraud_label
ytest  <- boost_test$fraud_label

set.seed(2026)

bart_model <- pbart(
  x.train = xtrain,
  y.train = ytrain,
  x.test = xtest
)

yhat_bart_prob <- bart_model$prob.test.mean

actual <- factor(ifelse(ytest == 1, "X1", "X0"), levels = c("X0", "X1"))

roc_obj <- roc(actual, yhat_bart_prob, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

thresh_tbl <- coords(
  roc_obj,
  x = "all",
  ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"),
  transpose = FALSE
)

thresh_tbl <- thresh_tbl[is.finite(thresh_tbl$threshold), ]
thresh_tbl$youden <- thresh_tbl$sensitivity + thresh_tbl$specificity - 1
best_thresh <- thresh_tbl$threshold[which.max(thresh_tbl$youden)]

bart_pred <- factor(ifelse(yhat_bart_prob >= best_thresh, "X1", "X0"),
                    levels = c("X0", "X1"))

confusionMatrix(bart_pred, actual, positive = "X1")
```

### Second BART Model

This BART model uses upSamples to increase performance

```{r bart2}
bart_train <- d1 |>
  mutate(fraud_label = ifelse(fraud_label == "X0", 0, 1)) |>
  as.data.frame()

bart_test <- test |>
  mutate(fraud_label = ifelse(fraud_label == "X0", 0, 1)) |>
  as.data.frame()

train_up <- upSample(
  x = bart_train |> dplyr::select(-fraud_label),
  y = factor(bart_train$fraud_label, levels = c(0, 1))
)

# upSample renames response to "Class"
train_up <- train_up |>
  mutate(fraud_label = ifelse(Class == "1", 1, 0)) |>
  dplyr::select(-Class)


xtrain2 <- model.matrix(fraud_label ~ . - 1, data = train_up)
ytrain2 <- train_up$fraud_label

xtest2 <- model.matrix(fraud_label ~ . - 1, data = bart_test)
ytest2 <- bart_test$fraud_label


set.seed(2026)

bart_model2 <- pbart(
  x.train = xtrain2,
  y.train = ytrain2,
  x.test  = xtest2,
  ntree = 100,
  ndpost = 1000,
  nskip = 200
)

bart_prob2 <- bart_model2$prob.test.mean

actual2 <- factor(ifelse(ytest2 == 1, "X1", "X0"), levels = c("X0", "X1"))


bart_pred2 <- ifelse(bart_prob2 >= 0.05, "X1", "X0")
bart_pred2 <- factor(bart_pred2, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

cm_bart <- confusionMatrix(bart_pred2, actual2, positive = "X1")

```


## RESULTS -------------------------------

Now I want to compare the results of the best models from the 4 different "Types" of models I used

```{r result_of_test}
get_metrics <- function(cm) {
  data.frame(
    Accuracy = as.numeric(cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
    Sensitivity = as.numeric(cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]),
    Specificity = as.numeric(cm$byClass["Specificity"]),
    Precision = as.numeric(cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]),
    F1 = as.numeric(cm$byClass["F1"])
  )
}

model_results <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "Logistic", get_metrics(cm_log)),
  cbind(Model = "KNN", get_metrics(cm_knn)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", get_metrics(cm_rf)),
  cbind(Model = "BART", get_metrics(cm_bart))
)

rownames(model_results) <- NULL

# model_results

# ai assisted in creating this table
library(kableExtra)

# round values
model_results_fmt <- model_results
model_results_fmt[,-1] <- round(model_results_fmt[,-1], 3)

# find best row (highest F1 or whatever you want)
best_row <- which.max(model_results_fmt$F1)

kable(model_results_fmt,
      caption = "Model Performance Comparison",
      align = "lccccc") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE,
                position = "center",
                bootstrap_options = c("striped")) %>%
  
  # HEADER STYLE (blue like your image)
  row_spec(0,
           bold = TRUE,
           color = "white",
           background = "#4F79A7",
           font_size = 22) %>%
  
  # ALTERNATING ROW COLORS (light gray)
  row_spec(1:nrow(model_results_fmt),
           background = ifelse(1:nrow(model_results_fmt) %% 2 == 0,
                               "#EDEFF2", "#D6DBE3")) %>%
  
  # HIGHLIGHT BEST MODEL (green)
  row_spec(best_row,
           background = "#00FF00",
           bold = TRUE)

```

### Select Best model

Among all models evaluated, logistic regression performed best for fraud detection. Although it had lower overall accuracy, it achieved the highest sensitivity and F1 score, making it the most effective at identifying fraudulent transactions. In contrast, models such as Random Forest achieved high accuracy but failed to detect fraud, demonstrating that accuracy alone is not an appropriate metric for this problem.

### Logistic Visualizations

ROC curve

```{r roc_curve_log}
library(pROC)

# predicted probabilities
log_probs <- predict(logistic3, newdata = test, type = "response")

# actual
actual <- factor(test$fraud_label, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

# ROC
roc_log <- roc(actual, log_probs, levels = c("X0", "X1"))

roc_df <- data.frame(
  fpr = 1 - roc_log$specificities,
  tpr = roc_log$sensitivities
)

# Sort by x-axis so the curve draws correctly
roc_df <- roc_df[order(roc_df$fpr), ]

# Plot
ggplot(roc_df, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color="red") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "ROC Curve - Logistic Regression",
    x = "1 - Specificity",
    y = "Sensitivity"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# AUC
auc(roc_log)
```
